name: Creativity
tagline: Find more ideas, beat creative block and make things people want to see.
description: Creativity is a skill you can practise, not a gift you either have or lack. These lessons cover generating ideas, getting unstuck, seeing like a photographer, telling stories, sharing your work and building a steady creative practice.

messages.welcome: You are more creative than you think. We will start small: one idea, one sketch, one photo at a time.
messages.comeback: Welcome back. No masterpiece needed today. Make one small, messy thing and the rest will follow.
messages.pass: Nicely done. You are starting to see the world like a maker.
messages.fail: First drafts are supposed to be rough. Read the explanations, look at the lesson again and give it another try.
messages.finished: You can now generate ideas on demand, push through creative block, compose a strong photo, shape a story, share your work and keep a practice going. Pick one small project and finish it this week.

lessons.title: Creativity is a skill, not a talent
lessons.content:
Creativity means making something new by joining old things together in a fresh way. Think of a cook. She doesn't invent rice, dal or onions. She mixes them in a new way and you get khichuri. A new song uses the same seven notes every song uses. So being creative is not magic. It's mixing.

Why does this matter? Because if you think creativity is a gift you're born with, you stop trying the moment something looks hard. You say "I'm not creative" and never draw, write or build anything. But if creativity is a skill, like riding a bicycle, then you just need practice. Every try makes the next one a little easier, and you start solving problems at school and at home in clever ways.

Here's how to practise. Rule one: collect pieces. The more things you see, read and try, the more pieces you have to mix. Watch how a rickshaw puller decorates his rickshaw. Notice the colours at the bazar. Every new thing you notice is a new piece in your box.

Rule two: do a small "what else?" game every day. Pick one ordinary object and ask "What else could this be?" A plastic bottle could be a pen holder, a plant pot, a piggy bank or a toy boat. Try to find five uses in two minutes. When you get stuck, change the size, the place or the person using it. That is exactly the muscle artists and inventors use.

Meet Nusrat, a class six student in Khulna. She always said, "I can't draw, my friend Tania is the creative one." Her teacher asked everyone to make a poster about saving water. Nusrat almost gave up. Then she tried the "what else?" game with a tap: what else could a tap be? A crying eye! She drew a tap shaped like an eye with a tear dripping out and wrote "Don't let it cry." Her poster got pinned on the school notice board. She didn't suddenly become talented. She just practised one trick.

The common mistake is comparing your first try with someone else's hundredth. Tania looks creative because she has drawn every day for years. You're seeing her practice, not her gift. Compare yourself only with yourself from last week.

Remember: creativity is mixing old pieces in new ways, and anyone who practises gets better at it.
key_points: Creativity means joining existing things in a new way.
It is a skill that grows with practice, like riding a bicycle.
Collect pieces by noticing things, and play the "what else could this be?" game.
Compare yourself with your own past, not with someone who has practised for years.
lessons.tip: When you hear yourself say "I'm not creative", change it to "I haven't practised this yet". Then do one two-minute "what else?" round.
lessons.task: Pick 3 objects near you, like a spoon, a bucket and an old newspaper. Set a 2-minute timer for each and write down as many new uses as you can.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what is creativity mostly?
options: A gift some people are born with
Joining old things together in a fresh way
quiz.explain: Like khichuri made from rice and dal, most new ideas are new mixes of things that already exist.

quiz.q: What is the "what else?" game?
options: Asking what else an ordinary object could be used for
Asking a friend what else to draw
quiz.explain: You pick an everyday object and find new uses for it, which trains your mixing muscle.

quiz.q: How did Nusrat make her water-saving poster?
options: She asked her teacher to draw it
She waited until she felt inspired
She asked what else a tap could be and drew it as a crying eye
quiz.explain: She used the "what else?" trick on a tap, got the crying-eye idea, and turned it into a poster.

lessons.title: Quantity first, quality later
lessons.content:
Here's a strange trick: if you want one great idea, make lots of ideas first. Think of fishing in a pond. If you throw one hook, you might catch nothing. If you throw a big net, you'll pull up lots of small fish, some old shoes, and maybe one big rui. Ideas work the same way. Your best idea is usually hiding somewhere in a long list.

Why? Because your first ideas are almost always the obvious ones, the same ones everyone else thinks of. If your teacher asks for a story about Eid, the first idea in every head is "I got new clothes and salami." By idea number ten, your brain has used up the easy stuff and starts making surprising links. Stop at idea one and you sound like everyone else. Keep going and you find something only you would think of.

Here's how. Step one: set a number and a timer. Say "10 ideas in 10 minutes." A number stops you from quitting early. Step two: write every idea down, even silly ones. Don't judge while you write. Judging and creating at the same time is like pressing the brake and the accelerator together. You go nowhere.

Step three: when the timer ends, then you judge. Read the list and circle your top two or three. Step four: mix or improve the circled ones. Often idea 3 plus idea 8 is better than either alone. So the order is simple: first make many, then pick, then polish.

Take Sabbir from Rajshahi. His class had to suggest a name and an idea for the school's science fair stall. Last year, he wrote the first thing that came to mind, "Volcano Model," and so did four other groups. This year he set a timer and forced himself to write 15 ideas. Idea 1 was volcano again. Idea 7 was "a fan that runs on a bicycle." Idea 12 was "rain alarm for the roof." He combined them into "Pedal Power Rain Alarm." The judges said it was the most original stall at the fair.

The most common mistake is throwing ideas away in your head before writing them down. You think "that's stupid" and skip it. But a stupid idea is often the stepping stone to a smart one. Write it, then move on. Bad ideas on paper cost nothing.

Remember: make lots of ideas first, judge them later, and your best one is rarely the first.
key_points: Your first ideas are usually the obvious ones everyone else has too.
Set a number and a timer, like 10 ideas in 10 minutes.
Write everything down without judging, then pick the best afterwards.
Mixing two ideas from your list often beats either one alone.
lessons.tip: Number your ideas 1 to 10 on the page before you start. Empty numbers push you to keep going until the list is full.
lessons.task: Set a 10-minute timer and write 10 ideas for something real: a gift for your mother, a name for a WhatsApp group, or a weekend plan. Circle your top two.

quiz.q: Why should you keep going past your first few ideas?
options: First ideas are usually the obvious ones, and surprising ideas come later
Teachers give marks for long lists
The first idea is always wrong
quiz.explain: Your brain uses up the easy, common ideas first, and fresher links appear after that.

quiz.q: Why should you not judge ideas while writing them?
options: Judging and creating together is like pressing the brake and accelerator at once
quiz.explain: Creating needs freedom and judging needs care, so doing both at once stops you moving.

quiz.q: What did Sabbir do differently this year?
options: He copied the volcano model again
He wrote 15 ideas with a timer and combined two of them
He asked his elder brother for an idea
He chose the first idea quickly
quiz.explain: He forced a long list, then mixed idea 7 and idea 12 into one original stall.

lessons.title: Mix and remix: combining ideas
lessons.content:
A lot of new ideas are just two old ideas holding hands. Think of a phone with a camera. Phones existed. Cameras existed. Someone put them together, and now almost everyone carries a camera in their pocket. Or think of fuchka: crispy shells plus spicy tamarind water. Two simple things, one famous street snack. Combining is the fastest way to make something that feels new.

Why does it help? Because staring at a blank page waiting for a brand new idea is slow and scary. Your brain doesn't create from nothing. It connects. When you give it two things to connect, ideas come quickly. Without this trick you keep waiting for "inspiration" and often make nothing. With it, you always have a way to start.

Here's how to do it. Step one: make two short lists. List A is about your topic. List B is something totally different. Say your topic is "a school bag." List A: straps, zip, pockets, books, water bottle. List B, pick anything random, like "rain": umbrella, puddles, thunder, frogs, rainbow.

Step two: join one item from each list and ask "What would that be?" Pocket plus umbrella: a bag with a fold-out rain cover. Zip plus rainbow: colour-coded zips so you know which pocket holds what. Straps plus frog: a bag that sits on your chest when crowded, like a frog on a leaf. Not every pair works, and that's fine. Try at least eight pairs. Step three: pick the best one and make it better. The further apart your two lists are, the more surprising the result.

Meet Tania from Sylhet. She wanted to start a small Facebook page selling her handmade bookmarks, but there were already many bookmark pages. She made List A: bookmark, paper, ribbon, page. For List B she chose "tea gardens," since she lives near them: leaves, tea cups, workers, hills. Bookmark plus tea leaf gave her an idea: bookmarks shaped like tea leaves, each with a real pressed leaf inside. Her page finally had something no other page had, and her first 20 pieces sold out in a week.

The common mistake is choosing List B too close to your topic. If your topic is "school bag" and List B is "pencil box," the ideas stay boring because the two things are already similar. Pick something far away, like food, animals, weather or a sport.

Remember: when you're stuck, take two different things and ask what happens when they meet.
key_points: Many new ideas are two old ideas joined together.
Make List A about your topic and List B about something unrelated.
Join one item from each list and ask "What would that be?"
The further apart the two lists, the more surprising the idea.
lessons.tip: Keep a jar of random words on paper slips, like "rain", "cricket", "kitchen", "train". When you need List B, pull one out without looking.
lessons.task: Pick an object you use daily. Write 5 parts of it in List A and 5 things about cricket in List B. Join 6 pairs and write one line for each idea.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of combining?
options: Joining two existing ideas to make something that feels new
Waiting for a brand new idea
Only using ideas from one topic
quiz.explain: Like phone plus camera, joining two existing things is a quick route to something new.

quiz.q: Which List B would give the most surprising ideas for a school bag?
quiz.explain: Things far from your topic give more surprising pairs. Things close to it keep ideas boring.

quiz.q: How did Tania make her bookmarks stand out?
options: She copied a popular bookmark page
She combined bookmarks with tea leaves from her area
quiz.explain: Joining her topic with "tea gardens" gave her tea-leaf bookmarks that no other page had.

lessons.title: Catch ideas before they vanish
lessons.content:
Ideas are like soap bubbles. They pop up suddenly, in the bath, on a rickshaw, just before sleep, and if you don't catch them, they're gone in seconds. An idea notebook is your bubble catcher. It's one place where every idea goes, the moment it appears.

Why bother? Because your brain is great at making ideas and terrible at storing them. You've probably had this happen: a brilliant thought comes on the bus, and by the time you get home you can only remember "it was something about birds." Without a catching system you lose most of your best thinking. With one, you build a bank of ideas you can use whenever you need to make something, so you never face an empty page again.

Here's how. Rule one: pick one place and only one. A small notebook in your bag or the notes app on a phone both work. If ideas are spread over five places, you'll never find them. Rule two: write it within ten seconds. Don't wait to get home. Even three words, like "fan powered boat," are enough to bring the idea back later.

Rule three: add one detail. Write where you were or what triggered it, like "saw a broken fan at the bazar." That small clue helps you remember the whole thought. Rule four: once a week, read the whole list. Takes five minutes. Put a star next to any idea that still excites you. Those starred ideas are your next projects.

Meet Rafi from Chattogram. He wanted to write stories for his school magazine, but whenever he sat down, his mind went blank. He started carrying a tiny notebook. On the bus he saw a man selling balloons in the rain, and wrote: "balloon seller, rain, nobody buying." At dinner his grandmother told a story about her village flood, and he wrote "Nanu, flood, saved the goat." On Friday he read his list, and those two notes joined into one story about a boy who uses balloons to float his goat during a flood. It was his first story printed in the magazine.

The common mistake is thinking "This idea is so good, I'll definitely remember it." You won't. Everyone believes that, and everyone forgets. The better the idea feels, the faster you should write it.

Remember: catch every idea in one place within ten seconds, and read your list once a week.
key_points: Ideas disappear within seconds if you don't write them down.
Use one place only, like a small notebook or a notes app.
Write the idea within ten seconds, plus one detail about where it came from.
Read the whole list once a week and star the ideas that still excite you.
lessons.tip: Start every note with today's date and a place, like "3 Oct, bus". The place often brings the whole memory back.
lessons.task: Get a notebook or open your phone's notes app and name a page "Ideas". Write down 3 ideas or interesting things you noticed today, each with one detail.

quiz.q: Why do you need an idea notebook?
options: Your brain is good at making ideas but bad at storing them
quiz.explain: Ideas come easily but vanish quickly, so you need a place to store them.

quiz.q: Which habit is part of the method?
options: Keeping ideas in five different apps
Writing the idea within ten seconds, in one place
Waiting until you get home to write
Only writing ideas that are already perfect
quiz.explain: One place and quick writing stop ideas from being lost or scattered.

quiz.q: How did Rafi get his first story?
options: He waited for inspiration at his desk
His grandmother wrote it for him
Two notes from his notebook joined into one story when he read his list
He copied a story from a magazine
quiz.explain: The balloon seller note and the flood note came together during his weekly read-through.

lessons.title: Why creative block happens
lessons.content:
Creative block is when you sit down to make something and nothing comes. You stare at the page, the pencil feels heavy, and your head feels empty. It's like a blocked water pipe. The water is still there, in your head, but something is stuck in the way.

Why should you understand it? Because if you think block means "I've run out of creativity," you'll quit. But block almost never means that. It usually has a clear cause, and once you know the cause, you can remove it. Knowing this turns a scary wall into a small problem you can fix in ten minutes.

There are four common causes, and each has a fix. Cause one: fear. You're worried it won't be good or people will laugh. Fix: tell yourself "this is just a practice version nobody will see." Cause two: the task is too big. "Write a story" is huge. Fix: make the first step tiny, like "write one sentence about a boy at a bus stop." Cause three: an empty tank. You've had no new input for days, just the same screens and routine. Fix: go and look at something new for fifteen minutes, then come back. Cause four: you're tired or hungry. Fix: eat, drink water, or rest first. A tired brain makes no ideas.

So when you're stuck, ask one question: "Which of the four is it?" Fear, too big, empty tank, or tired. Then try that fix. If you're not sure, start with the tiny-step fix. It works for most blocks.

Meet Sabbir from Dhaka. He had to make a short video for a school competition about traffic. He sat with his phone for two evenings and filmed nothing. He felt useless. On the third day he asked himself the question. The answer was "too big": he was trying to plan the whole video at once. So he set a tiny goal: "film just one shot of a rickshaw stuck in the jam." He went to the corner near his house and filmed it. Seeing that one clip gave him the next idea, then the next. In one week the whole video was done, and it won second prize.

The common mistake is waiting for the block to go away by itself. Scrolling, waiting for a mood, telling yourself you'll start "when you feel like it." Block gets stronger when you wait. It gets weaker the moment you do something small.

Remember: block has a cause, so name it, then take one tiny step.
key_points: Creative block is something stuck in the way, not an empty well.
The four common causes are fear, a task that's too big, no new input, and being tired.
Name the cause, then apply its fix.
When unsure, shrink the first step until it feels easy.
lessons.tip: Write the four causes on a sticky note near your desk: "Fear? Too big? Empty tank? Tired?" When stuck, read it and tick one.
lessons.task: Think of one thing you've been putting off making or writing. Decide which of the four causes is blocking it, and do a 10-minute tiny first step right now.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what does creative block usually mean?
options: You have run out of creativity forever
Something is in the way, and it has a cause you can fix
You should switch to a different hobby
quiz.explain: Block is like a blocked pipe: the ideas are still there, but something is stuck.

quiz.q: A task feels huge, like "make a whole video". What is the best fix?
options: Make the first step tiny, like filming one shot
Work all night without a break
Give the job to someone else
quiz.explain: Shrinking the first step removes the "too big" cause and gets you moving.

quiz.q: What finally helped Sabbir make his traffic video?
options: Naming the cause as "too big" and filming one rickshaw shot
quiz.explain: Once he set a tiny goal, the first clip led him to the next ideas.

lessons.title: Limits make you more creative
lessons.content:
A constraint is a limit or a rule, like "only 3 colours" or "only 50 words" or "only things you can find at home." It sounds like limits would kill creativity. Actually, they do the opposite. Imagine someone says "cook anything." You freeze. Now imagine "cook something using only eggs, onions and leftover rice." Suddenly your brain starts working: egg fried rice, an omelette with rice inside, rice pakora. The limit gave you a starting point.

Why does this work? Too many choices make your brain freeze, because you can't pick from everything at once. A limit cuts the choices down to a size your brain can handle. It also forces you away from your usual ideas, because your usual ideas often break the rule. Without limits, people often start nothing or make the same thing as always. With limits, they finish faster and come up with surprising solutions.

Here's how to use it. Step one: when a task feels too open, add one or two rules yourself. There are four easy kinds. A material limit: "only pencil," "only things from the kitchen." A size limit: "one page," "a 30-second video," "exactly 6 words." A time limit: "finish in 20 minutes." A rule limit: "no talking in the video," "no letter E," "only black and white."

Step two: pick a limit that pushes you a little, not one that makes the task impossible. Step three: stick to it. The moment you break the rule, you're back to too many choices. If a limit truly doesn't work after a fair try, swap it for another one, but don't just drop all rules.

Meet Nusrat from Barishal. She wanted to make an Eid card for her nana, but she'd been "planning" it for a week and had made nothing, because she couldn't decide on a design. Her elder sister gave her a challenge: "Use only things from the kitchen and finish in 30 minutes." Nusrat looked around and found turmeric, red chilli powder, and some rice. She painted with turmeric water, made a red border with chilli paste, and glued rice grains into the words "Eid Mubarak." Her nana kept that card on his shelf all year.

The common mistake is making the limit so tight the task becomes impossible, like "write a story in 2 words in 1 minute." Then you just get frustrated. A good limit should feel like a fun puzzle, not a wall.

Remember: when you have too many choices, add a rule, and let the rule push your brain to new ideas.
key_points: A constraint is a limit or rule, like only 3 colours or only 50 words.
Too many choices freeze your brain; limits give it a starting point.
Use material, size, time or rule limits.
Choose a limit that feels like a puzzle, not an impossible wall.
lessons.tip: If you can't start, write "Only ___ in ___ minutes" at the top of the page and fill in the blanks before you do anything else.
lessons.task: Write a story about your day in exactly 6 words. Then take one photo using only the colour blue. Give yourself 10 minutes for both.

quiz.q: Why do limits often help creativity?
options: They make work look more serious
They cut choices down so your brain can start
quiz.explain: Too many choices freeze the brain. A limit narrows them to a size you can work with.

quiz.q: Which of these is a size limit?
quiz.explain: A size limit controls how big or long the work is, like 30 seconds or one page.

quiz.q: What limit helped Nusrat finally finish her Eid card?
options: Only things from the kitchen, finished in 30 minutes
Copying a card from the internet
Working on it for another week
quiz.explain: The material limit plus a time limit gave her a clear puzzle, so she made the card fast.

lessons.title: Fill the well: input and curiosity
lessons.content:
Think of your mind as a well. Every idea you make is a bucket of water pulled out. If nothing new goes in, the well slowly dries up. Input is everything that fills it: books, walks, conversations, music, museums, watching how things work. Curiosity is the habit of noticing and asking "why?" and "how?" so that more water flows in every day.

Why does it matter? Because ideas are made by mixing pieces, and you can only mix what you've collected. If you watch the same kind of video every day, all your pieces look the same, and so do your ideas. People who feel "dried up" have often just had the same input for weeks. When you fill the well with different things, ideas start coming without forcing.

Here's how to fill it. Rule one: mix your input. Each week, try to get something from at least three different areas: something to read, something to watch or listen to, and something real in the world, like a walk through the bazar or talking to a grandparent. Different areas give you pieces nobody else is mixing.

Rule two: look closely, not just more. When you're out, pick one thing and study it for a minute. How does the tea stall owner pour tea from high up without spilling? Why are some rickshaws painted with film stars? Rule three: ask people questions. Every adult knows things you don't. Ask your uncle how he fixes motors, ask the shopkeeper which item sells most. Rule four: write down what you notice in your idea notebook, so it doesn't leak out.

Meet Tania from Mymensingh. She loved drawing comics, but all her characters started to look like the cartoons she watched every day. She felt she had no new ideas. So for two weeks she changed her input. She read a book about the Sundarbans, watched her mother make pitha, and asked her grandfather about his childhood in a village with no electricity. She wrote little notes each day. Her next comic was about a girl who lights her village with fireflies from the Sundarbans. Her friends said it was her best one, because it felt like nothing they'd seen.

The common mistake is thinking input means endless scrolling. Scrolling feels like input, but it's usually the same short clips over and over, chosen for you, and you forget them in minutes. Real input is chosen by you, a bit slower, and different from your usual stuff.

Remember: ideas come out only after pieces go in, so keep filling your well with different, real things.
key_points: Input is everything that fills your mind: books, walks, people, music, places.
Same input every day leads to the same ideas.
Mix input from at least three different areas each week.
Look closely, ask people questions, and write down what you notice.
lessons.tip: Next time you're at the bazar or on a rickshaw, pick one thing and ask yourself "how does this work?" for a full minute.
lessons.task: Ask an older family member one question about their childhood, like what they played or ate. Listen for 10 minutes and write 3 details in your idea notebook.

quiz.q: Why does the same input every day make ideas weaker?
options: Your brain gets tired of reading
You can only mix the pieces you've collected, so same pieces give same ideas
Input has nothing to do with ideas
quiz.explain: Ideas are mixes of pieces, so if all your pieces look the same, your ideas will too.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of "looking closely"?
options: Studying how a tea seller pours tea from high up for a minute
Reading only the titles of books
quiz.explain: Looking closely means studying one thing carefully and asking how it works.

quiz.q: How did Tania get new comic ideas?
options: She stopped drawing for a month
She read, watched her mother make pitha and asked her grandfather questions
quiz.explain: Changing her input to different, real things gave her the firefly village idea.

lessons.title: Make it bad on purpose
lessons.content:
Here's a strange trick: when you can't start because you want it to be perfect, try to make it as bad as possible on purpose. Draw the worst cat ever. Write the most boring opening line in history. It sounds silly, but it's like jumping into a cold pond. Once you're in, the water doesn't feel so scary anymore.

Why does this work? Because the biggest thing stopping most people is fear of making something bad. That fear makes your hand freeze before you even start. When you aim for "bad," you can't fail, so the fear switches off. Your hand moves, your brain wakes up, and very often, something good sneaks in. Without this trick, you might spend a whole evening staring at an empty page. With it, you're working within one minute.

Here's how. Step one: say out loud, "This is the bad version." Step two: set a short timer, like 5 minutes, and make the worst version you can. Write clichés, draw wobbly lines, use ugly colours. Have fun with it. Step three: when the timer ends, look at it and circle anything that's actually interesting, even one line or one shape. There's almost always something.

Step four: start your real version, using what you circled. You're no longer starting from zero. You're improving something, and improving is much easier than starting. Many writers and designers call this "the ugly first draft," and they all make one.

Meet Rafi from Cumilla. He had a Bangla essay due about "My favourite season." He wanted it to be the best in class, so he kept writing the first line and deleting it. After an hour he had nothing. His tutor told him, "Write the worst essay you can in 5 minutes." Laughing, Rafi wrote: "Monsoon is wet. Wet is bad. My socks are always wet." When he read it back, he realised the wet socks line was actually funny and true. He started his real essay with the story of his socks never drying in monsoon, then wrote about the smell of rain and khichuri days. His teacher read it to the whole class.

The common mistake is showing the bad version to everyone and feeling embarrassed, or treating it as the final work. The bad version is just a warm-up, only for you. Its job is to get you moving, not to impress anyone.

Remember: when perfect is stopping you, make it bad on purpose, then build the good version from what you find.
key_points: Fear of making something bad is what stops most people from starting.
Aiming for a bad version switches the fear off, because you can't fail.
Set a 5-minute timer, make the worst version, then circle anything interesting.
Build your real version from what you circled, so you're improving, not starting.
lessons.tip: Write "BAD VERSION" in big letters at the top of the page. It's a reminder that this page is allowed to be ugly.
lessons.task: Set a 5-minute timer and draw the worst possible picture of your house or write the worst possible poem about rain. Then circle one part you actually like.

quiz.q: Why does making something bad on purpose help you start?
options: You can't fail at being bad, so the fear of failing switches off
quiz.explain: When the goal is "bad", there's nothing to fear, so your hand starts moving.

quiz.q: After the timer ends on your bad version, what should you do?
options: Circle anything interesting and use it to start the real version
quiz.explain: The bad version often hides a good line or shape that becomes your starting point.

quiz.q: What did Rafi find in his bad essay?
options: A full essay he could submit
A funny, true line about wet socks that became his opening
quiz.explain: His silly sentence about wet socks gave him a real, fresh way to start his monsoon essay.

lessons.title: Learn to see light
lessons.content:
A photo is really a picture of light. The camera doesn't see your friend's face. It sees the light bouncing off it. So the same face can look tired and flat in one photo and glowing in the next, just because the light changed. Learning to see light is like learning to hear the difference between a whisper and a shout.

Why does it matter? Because most bad photos aren't bad because of the phone. They're bad because of the light. Harsh noon sun makes people squint and gives them dark shadows under their eyes. A bright window behind someone turns them into a dark blob. Once you notice light, the same cheap phone suddenly takes much better pictures, for free.

Here's what to look for. One: the direction. Light from the side shows shape and texture, like the rough skin of a jackfruit. Light from the front is flat and safe. Light from behind the subject makes a glowing outline, or a silhouette if the background is very bright. Two: hard or soft. Direct sun at noon is hard: sharp shadows, bright spots. Cloudy days or shade give soft light: gentle shadows, smooth faces. For portraits, soft is usually kinder.

Three: the time of day. The hour after sunrise and the hour before sunset are called the golden hour. The sun is low, so light is warm, soft and comes from the side. Almost everything looks better then. Midday is the hardest time; if you must shoot then, move your subject into shade. Four: when you can, move yourself or your subject, not the light. Turn your friend so the window light falls on their face, not behind them.

Meet Nusrat from Rangpur. She took photos of her mother's handmade nakshi kantha to sell on Facebook, but the pictures looked dull and nobody asked about them. She was shooting at 1 pm in the courtyard with harsh sun. Her cousin suggested trying again near a window in the late afternoon. Nusrat laid the kantha near the window, with light coming from the side. Suddenly every stitch threw a tiny shadow, and you could see the texture. The colours looked warm and rich. That week, five people messaged asking for the price.

The common mistake is putting your subject in front of a bright window or the sun, then wondering why their face is dark. The camera sets itself for the bright part, so the face goes black. Turn around so the light falls on the face.

Remember: before you press the button, look at where the light is coming from, and move until it falls the way you want.
key_points: A photo is a picture of light, so changing the light changes the whole photo.
Side light shows texture, front light is flat, back light makes outlines or silhouettes.
Soft light from clouds or shade is kinder to faces than hard noon sun.
The golden hour, just after sunrise and before sunset, gives warm, soft light.
lessons.tip: Before taking a portrait, turn your friend slowly in a circle and watch their face on the screen. Stop when the light looks best.
lessons.task: Take 3 photos of the same object, like a fruit or a cup: one near a window with side light, one with light from behind it, and one under the ceiling light. Compare them.

quiz.q: Why do many photos of people look bad at noon?
options: Hard overhead sun makes them squint and gives dark eye shadows
Phones don't work well at noon
quiz.explain: Midday sun is hard and from above, which creates harsh shadows and squinting.

quiz.q: When is the golden hour?
options: In the middle of the night
The hour after sunrise and the hour before sunset
quiz.explain: The low sun at those times gives warm, soft, side light.

quiz.q: What change made Nusrat's kantha photos better?
options: She moved it near a window in the late afternoon with side light
She added a filter at noon
She shot it from very far away
quiz.explain: Soft side light from the window showed every stitch's texture and warmed the colours.

lessons.title: Composition: rule of thirds and leading lines
lessons.content:
Composition means where you put things inside your photo. Think of arranging food on a plate. The same rice, fish and salad can look messy or beautiful depending on where you place them. Two simple tools help a lot: the rule of thirds and leading lines.

Why bother? Because most people put the main thing dead centre and leave the rest to chance. The photo often feels stiff, and the eye doesn't know where to go. Good composition guides the viewer's eye, makes the photo feel balanced, and makes a simple scene look planned and interesting. It costs nothing, just a few seconds of thinking before you tap.

Here's the rule of thirds. Imagine two lines across your screen and two lines down, like a noughts-and-crosses grid, making nine boxes. Instead of putting your subject in the very middle, put it on one of the lines, or where two lines cross. Put the horizon on the top line or the bottom line, not across the middle. If the sky is beautiful, give it two thirds. If the land or river is the interesting part, give that two thirds. Most phones can show this grid: turn on "Grid" in the camera settings.

Now leading lines. These are lines in the scene that pull the eye towards your subject: a road, a railway track, a riverbank, a row of trees, a wall, even a line of rickshaws. Stand so the line starts near a corner or the bottom of your frame and runs towards the subject. The viewer's eye will slide along it like a train on a track and land right where you want. Best of all, combine the two: a road leading to a person standing on a third line.

Meet Sabbir from Sirajganj. He took a photo of his little brother flying a kite in a field, but in the picture the boy was a tiny dot in the centre and the horizon cut the photo in half. It looked empty. He turned on the grid, walked to the end of the field's narrow mud path, and crouched. Now the path ran from the bottom corner to his brother, who stood on the right third line, with the sky taking the top two thirds and the kite high in it. His father made it his phone wallpaper.

The common mistake is following the rules so strictly you forget the subject. Some things, like a perfectly symmetrical mosque or a face looking straight at you, look great in the centre. The rules are a starting point. If centring looks better, centre it.

Remember: turn on the grid, put your subject on a third, and use lines to lead the eye to it.
key_points: Composition means where you place things in the frame.
Rule of thirds: put the subject on a grid line, not dead centre, and keep the horizon off the middle.
Leading lines like roads, rails or rivers guide the eye to your subject.
The rules are a starting point; symmetrical scenes can look great centred.
lessons.tip: Turn on the grid in your phone's camera settings today. It stays on, so every future photo gets the thirds lines for free.
lessons.task: Turn on your camera grid and take 2 photos of the same thing: one with it in the centre, one on a third line with a leading line pointing to it. Compare which feels better.

quiz.q: Where does the rule of thirds suggest putting your subject?
options: On one of the grid lines or where they cross
quiz.explain: Placing the subject on a third line usually feels more balanced and interesting than dead centre.

quiz.q: Which of these is a leading line?
options: A railway track running towards a person
quiz.explain: A railway track is a line in the scene that pulls the eye towards the subject.

quiz.q: What made Sabbir's kite photo better?
options: A mud path leading to his brother on the right third, with sky in the top two thirds
Putting his brother in the centre with the horizon in the middle
quiz.explain: He combined a leading line with the rule of thirds instead of a centred tiny dot.

lessons.title: Framing, angles and empty space
lessons.content:
Three more tools make ordinary photos look special. Framing means shooting through something, like a doorway, a window or tree branches, so it makes a "frame inside the frame." Angle means where your camera is: high, low, or at eye level. Negative space means leaving empty, quiet space around your subject, like plain sky or a blank wall. Think of them like seasoning: same food, much more flavour.

Why use them? Because most people take every photo standing up, at their own eye level, with the subject filling a busy background. All those photos look the same. Changing one of these three things makes people stop and look. A frame tells the viewer exactly where to look. An unusual angle shows the world in a way people don't normally see. Empty space makes the subject stand out and feel calm or lonely, depending on what you want.

Here's how to use each. Framing: look for natural frames around your subject. A window with your grandmother sitting inside it. Your friend seen through the gap in a bamboo fence. A boat seen between two tree trunks. Keep the frame a bit darker or blurrier, and the subject in focus.

Angles: try three heights before you choose. Go low, close to the ground, and shoot up. It makes things look tall and powerful, great for buildings or a cricketer about to bowl. Go high and shoot down. It makes things look small, or shows patterns, like plates of food on a table. For children and pets, crouch to their eye level; it makes the photo feel personal. Negative space: put your small subject in one part of the frame and leave the rest empty. A single boat on a wide, calm river. One bird on a long electric wire.

Meet Tania from Cox's Bazar. She wanted a photo for a school contest called "My Town." Everyone was sending the same beach photo taken standing up. Tania crouched down on the sand so the waves looked huge, then waited until a fisherman's boat sat alone on the right side of the empty sea. For a second shot, she framed a fish seller through the open door of a tea stall. Her teacher picked the lone boat photo for the school wall, saying it "felt peaceful."

The common mistake is leaving empty space that isn't really empty: a messy background full of wires, signboards and people. Empty space only works when it's plain. Move your feet or change the angle until the background is simple.

Remember: shoot through a frame, try a high and a low angle, and give your subject room to breathe.
key_points: Framing means shooting through a door, window or branches so the subject has a frame.
Low angles make things look big, high angles show patterns, eye level feels personal.
Negative space is plain empty space that makes a small subject stand out.
Empty space only works if the background is actually plain, not cluttered.
lessons.tip: Before every photo, take one extra shot from very low and one from above. It takes 5 seconds and often the extra shot is the best.
lessons.task: Take 3 photos of one thing at home: one through a door or window as a frame, one from floor level, and one with lots of empty wall or sky around it.

quiz.q: What is framing in photography?
options: Putting the photo in a wooden frame
Shooting through something like a door or branches so the subject has a frame
Taking a photo from very high
quiz.explain: A natural frame inside the photo tells the viewer exactly where to look.

quiz.q: What does shooting from a low angle usually do?
options: Makes the subject look tall and powerful
quiz.explain: Shooting up from low makes buildings and people look big and strong.

quiz.q: Why did Tania's lone boat photo stand out?
options: She used the same standing-up shot as everyone
She added many people around the boat
She zoomed in on the boat only
She crouched low and placed the boat alone in plenty of empty sea
quiz.explain: A low angle plus negative space made her photo look different and calm.

lessons.title: Colour and contrast
lessons.content:
Colour is the feeling of a photo. Contrast is the difference between things: light next to dark, or one colour next to a very different one. Think of a red flower in a green field. Your eye goes straight to it, because red and green are very different. That pull is contrast, and it's one of the strongest tools you have.

Why does it matter? Because the human eye always jumps to the part of a picture that's most different from the rest. If everything is the same brightness and colour, the eye has nowhere to land and the photo feels dull. If too many bright colours fight each other, the photo feels messy. Understanding colour and contrast lets you decide where people look and what they feel.

Here's how to use colour. One: warm colours, like red, orange and yellow, feel energetic and cosy. Cool colours, like blue and green, feel calm. Choose based on the mood you want. Two: colours opposite each other on the colour wheel make strong contrast. The main pairs are blue and orange, red and green, and yellow and purple. A girl in an orange dress against a blue wall pops right out. Three: limit your colours. A photo with one or two main colours usually looks cleaner than one with seven.

Now light and dark contrast. Put a bright subject against a dark background, or a dark subject against a bright one, and it stands out instantly. A white egret on dark water. A dark tree against a bright evening sky. One more trick: if a scene is too colourful and messy, try turning the photo black and white. Then only light and dark are left, and you can see if the photo is strong without colour.

Meet Rafi from Narayanganj. He took photos of his cousin's small fruit stall for its Facebook page, but the fruit looked like a jumble. He tried something new. He put the yellow mangoes in a blue plastic bowl, and placed red tomatoes next to green chillies for a second shot. Each photo had just two main colours, and they were opposites. Then he shot against the dark shop wall so the fruit glowed. His cousin said the posts got more comments than ever before.

The common mistake is adding colour with heavy filters and maximum saturation. The colours start looking fake, skin turns orange, and the photo looks cheap. Instead, get the colour right while shooting: choose the background, the clothes and the light. Edit only a little.

Remember: use opposite colours or light against dark to pull the eye, and keep to one or two main colours.
key_points: Contrast is difference, and the eye always jumps to the most different part of a photo.
Warm colours feel energetic, cool colours feel calm.
Opposite pairs like blue and orange or red and green make a subject pop.
Bright against dark makes a subject stand out; don't fake colour with heavy filters.
lessons.tip: When choosing a background for a portrait, pick the colour opposite to what the person is wearing: blue wall for an orange shirt, green leaves for a red dress.
lessons.task: Find two objects at home in opposite colours, like an orange and a blue cup. Photograph them together against a plain background, then take the same photo in black and white.

quiz.q: Which pair of colours makes strong contrast?
quiz.explain: Blue and orange are opposite on the colour wheel, so they make each other pop.

quiz.q: What does a white egret on dark water show?
quiz.explain: A bright subject against a dark background stands out instantly.

quiz.q: How did Rafi make the fruit stall photos better?
options: He used the strongest filter and full saturation
He photographed all the fruits together in one jumble
He used pairs of opposite colours and a dark wall behind the fruit
He shot only in black and white
quiz.explain: Two opposite main colours and light-against-dark contrast made each photo clean and eye-catching.

lessons.title: Every story needs a change
lessons.content:
A story is not just a list of things that happened. It's about something changing. Compare these two. "I woke up, ate breakfast, went to school and came home." That's a list. Now: "I was scared of the school bus bully, until one day I stood up to him." That's a story, because something changed: you went from scared to brave. Change is the heartbeat of every story.

Why does it matter? Because without change, people get bored and stop listening, even if the events are exciting. A cricket match where nothing is at stake is dull. A story where the character is the same at the end as at the start feels pointless. Change gives people a reason to keep reading: they want to know how it turns out. It also makes your story feel meaningful, because change is what real life is about.

Here's how to build change into a story. Step one: decide how your main character is at the start. What do they want, fear or believe? Example: "Rina wants to win the art competition but thinks her drawings are worse than everyone's." Step two: give them a problem or obstacle that pushes them. "Her paints get ruined by rain the night before."

Step three: show how they deal with it. "She uses tea, turmeric and charcoal from the kitchen to paint instead." Step four: decide how they are different at the end. Did they get what they wanted? Learn something? Change their mind? "She doesn't win first prize, but she learns her ideas are special, and she stops comparing herself to others." A quick test: finish this sentence, "At the start ___, but by the end ___." If you can't fill it in, your story needs a change.

Meet Sabbir from Bogura. He wrote a story for his class about a trip to his grandfather's village. It went: they took the bus, ate lunch, saw the fields, came home. His teacher gave him average marks and wrote, "What changed?" Sabbir thought about it. Actually, on that trip, he'd been afraid of cows, and his grandfather taught him to feed one. He rewrote the story around that: a city boy scared of cows, a calf that wouldn't leave him alone, and by the end, him crying when he had to say goodbye to it. The second version got the highest mark in class.

The common mistake is making the change happen by luck, like the problem just disappears or someone else solves it. Readers feel cheated. The change should come from the character's own choice or action.

Remember: every story needs a change, so ask "what's different at the end?"
key_points: A story is about something changing, not just a list of events.
Decide how the character starts, what problem they face, and how they end up different.
Test it with: "At the start ___, but by the end ___."
The change should come from the character's own choice, not luck.
lessons.tip: Before writing any story, write the "At the start ___, but by the end ___" sentence at the top of your page. Then write towards it.
lessons.task: Think of one small real moment from your life where you changed, like learning to swim or making a new friend. Write it in 5 sentences using the start-problem-action-end steps.

quiz.q: What makes something a story instead of a list?
options: Something changes from the start to the end
quiz.explain: Change is what turns a list of events into a story people want to follow.

quiz.q: Which sentence helps you test if your story has a change?
options: "At the start ___, but by the end ___."
quiz.explain: If you can fill in both blanks, your character has changed.

quiz.q: Why did Sabbir's second story get the highest mark?
options: It had more places in it
He built it around his change from being scared of cows to loving a calf
It was copied from a book
quiz.explain: The first version was a list. The second showed a real change in him.

lessons.title: Story structure: beginning, middle, end
lessons.content:
Story structure is the shape of a story: a beginning, a middle and an end. Think of a journey by train from Dhaka to Chattogram. At the start you board and settle in. In the middle, things happen: delays, a crying baby, a stranger sharing jhalmuri. At the end, you arrive somewhere new. Without the start, people are confused. Without the middle, nothing happens. Without the end, they feel cheated.

Why does it matter? Because a story without shape feels like someone rambling. You've heard a friend tell a story where they keep saying "oh wait, I forgot to tell you..." and you lose track. A clear structure makes your story easy to follow and keeps tension rising until the end. It works for an essay, a short film, a speech, a comic and even a Facebook post.

Here's how to build each part. The beginning, about one fifth of the story: introduce who, where and what they want. Then add the trouble, the thing that kicks the story into motion. "Mitu wanted to buy a gift for her mother's birthday. But she had only 50 taka, and the birthday was tomorrow." Start close to the trouble. Don't spend half the story on the weather.

The middle, the biggest part: the character tries to solve the problem, and things get harder. Use the "try, fail, try again" pattern. Mitu tries to sell her old books, but nobody buys. She tries to make a card, but spills water on it. Each try raises the stakes. The end, short and satisfying: the biggest moment, where the problem is solved or not, then a few lines showing what changed. Mitu makes a breakfast of her mother's favourite paratha and writes a poem on a paper plate. Her mother cries happy tears and keeps the plate for years. Then stop. Don't drag on.

Meet Nusrat from Jessore. She had 3 minutes to tell a story at her school's speech day. In practice, she spent two minutes describing her family and her house, then rushed the actual event, losing her bicycle at the bazar, in 30 seconds. Her friends looked bored. She restructured: 30 seconds to set up, 2 minutes on the search, checking every shop, a rickshaw puller helping, and false hope when she saw a similar bike, and 30 seconds for finding it and what she learned. On the day, the hall went quiet as she spoke and clapped loudly at the end.

The common mistake is a beginning that's too long. People pack in background before anything happens, and the listener checks out. Get to the trouble quickly. You can add background later in the middle, little by little.

Remember: set up fast, make the middle a series of tries that get harder, and end with the big moment and what changed.
key_points: A story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
Beginning: who, where, what they want, and the trouble, kept short.
Middle: try, fail, try again, with things getting harder.
End: the big moment and what changed, then stop.
lessons.tip: Plan a story as three sentences first: one for the beginning, one for the middle, one for the end. If the three sentences work, the full story will too.
lessons.task: Think of one problem you had this month, like a lost item or a late bus. Write three sentences: beginning with the trouble, middle with two tries, end with what changed.

quiz.q: What should the beginning of a story include?
options: Who, where, what they want, and the trouble
Every detail about the character's family
Only a description of the weather
quiz.explain: The beginning sets up the character and the problem, then moves quickly to the trouble.

quiz.q: Which pattern makes the middle of a story exciting?
options: Try, fail, try again, with things getting harder
quiz.explain: Each failed try raises the stakes and keeps the reader wanting to know what happens.

quiz.q: What did Nusrat change in her speech-day story?
options: She added more about her house
She made the beginning short and gave most of the time to the search
quiz.explain: She stopped spending most of the time on background and put the action in the middle.

lessons.title: Show, don't tell
lessons.content:
"Show, don't tell" means letting readers see what's happening instead of just telling them the answer. "Rafi was nervous" is telling. "Rafi wiped his sweaty hands on his school trousers for the third time and kept checking the door" is showing. With telling, the reader just gets a label. With showing, they watch a little movie in their head and figure out the feeling themselves.

Why does it matter? Because telling is quick but flat. Words like "sad," "happy," "beautiful" or "scary" have been used so often that readers slide right over them. Showing makes people feel the emotion, not just know about it. It makes your writing memorable, and it works in essays, stories, captions and even messages to friends. Teachers notice it immediately.

Here's how to do it. Step one: find the telling words in your writing. Look for feelings (angry, scared, excited) and judgements (beautiful, delicious, boring). Step two: for each one, ask "How would I know?" If someone is angry, what do they do? Maybe they slam a door, speak through their teeth, or go red in the face. If food is delicious, what happens? Everyone goes quiet, someone licks their fingers, the plate is empty in two minutes.

Step three: use the senses. What do you see, hear, smell, taste, touch? "The bazar was busy" becomes "A man shouted 'Fresh hilsa, fresh!' over the honking, and I had to squeeze sideways between sacks of onions." Step four: use specific details, not general ones. Not "a bird" but "a crow," not "food" but "hot beef tehari." Don't show everything, though. Use it for the important moments and tell the boring connecting bits quickly, like "Two hours later, we reached home."

Meet Tania from Gazipur. Her essay about Eid said: "Eid was very fun. The food was delicious and I was happy." Her teacher wrote "Show me!" in the margin. Tania asked herself, "How would I know it was fun?" She rewrote it: "By ten in the morning my pocket crackled with new notes from salami. Nanu's kitchen smelled of cardamom and fried onions, and my cousins and I fought over the last piece of shemai." Her teacher gave her full marks and said she could almost smell the shemai.

The common mistake is overdoing it: three long sentences to show someone opening a door. Readers get tired. Show the moments that matter, keep it short, and tell the rest.

Remember: instead of naming a feeling, show what someone would see, hear or do that proves it.
key_points: Telling gives a label like "nervous"; showing gives details that prove it.
Ask "How would I know?" for every feeling or judgement word.
Use the senses and specific details, like "crow" instead of "bird".
Show the important moments, tell the boring connecting parts quickly.
lessons.tip: Circle every feeling word in your next essay, like "happy" or "scared". Replace at least two with an action or a sense detail.
lessons.task: Rewrite these three sentences by showing: "My mother was angry." "The rain was heavy." "The tea stall was busy." Use one action or sense detail in each.

quiz.q: Which sentence shows instead of tells?
options: Rafi wiped his sweaty hands on his trousers and kept checking the door
quiz.explain: Sweaty hands and checking the door let the reader see the nervousness for themselves.

quiz.q: What question helps you turn telling into showing?
quiz.explain: Asking how you'd know someone is angry or food is delicious leads you to the details.

quiz.q: What did Tania add to her Eid essay?
options: A list of everyone she met
Details like crackling salami notes, the smell of cardamom and fighting over shemai
quiz.explain: Sense details and specific actions made the reader feel Eid instead of being told it was fun.

lessons.title: Visual storytelling: a story in photos
lessons.content:
A photo story is a short set of pictures, usually 5 to 7, that tells a story when you look at them in order. Think of a comic strip without words. One photo shows a moment. A series shows what happened before, during and after, so people understand the whole story without anyone explaining.

Why does it matter? Because a single photo can only say so much. If you post one picture of your mother's cake, people see a cake. If you post a series, flour on her hands, the oven, your little sister trying to sneak a taste, the candles, the family laughing, people feel the day. Photo stories are used by journalists, on Facebook and Instagram, in school projects and at weddings. They help you share experiences instead of just objects.

Here's how to make one. Step one: pick a small story with a clear change, like making pitha, a cricket match on the street, or a day at grandmother's village. Step two: plan your shot types. You need three kinds. A wide shot sets the scene: the whole kitchen, the whole field. A medium shot shows people doing things: your mother rolling dough, the bowler running in. A close-up shows small details that carry feeling: hands shaping pitha, a cricket ball in the dust, a child's grin.

Step three: shoot more than you need, maybe 30 photos, following the story from start to finish. Look for one key moment, the peak, like the winning shot or the first bite. Step four: pick 5 to 7 photos. A simple order that works: start wide to set the scene, then medium shots of the action, then a close-up for feeling, then your key moment, and finally an ending shot that shows the result, like empty plates or a tired, happy team. Cut any photo that repeats another. Each photo should add something new.

Meet Rafi from Sunamganj. His class had a project: "Tell a story in photos." At first he posted 12 photos of his village's boat race, all wide shots from the same spot on the bank. It looked repetitive. He went again the next year with a plan. He took a wide shot of the river full of people, medium shots of rowers pulling together, a close-up of an old man's hands gripping the oar, the moment the winning boat crossed the line, and the team splashing water on each other. Six photos. His teacher said it was the first project where she felt like she was there.

The common mistake is using only one type of shot, usually wide, from one place. The photos all look the same. Move closer, move around, and mix wide, medium and close-up.

Remember: plan a small story, mix wide, medium and close-up shots, and choose 5 to 7 that each add something new.
key_points: A photo story is 5 to 7 photos that tell a story in order.
Use wide shots to set the scene, medium shots for action, close-ups for feeling.
Shoot more than you need and catch one key moment.
Cut repeats; every photo should add something new.
lessons.tip: While shooting, say the shot type in your head before each photo: "wide, medium, close." It stops you taking 20 photos from one spot.
lessons.task: Make a 5-photo story of something small at home, like making tea: one wide, two medium, one close-up and one ending photo. Put them in order and look at them as a set.

quiz.q: What does a close-up shot do in a photo story?
options: Shows small details that carry feeling
quiz.explain: Close-ups like hands gripping an oar add emotion and detail.

quiz.q: What is a good number of photos for a photo story?
quiz.explain: 5 to 7 photos are enough to tell a story without repeating yourself.

quiz.q: Why did Rafi's first boat race photo story look repetitive?
options: All 12 photos were wide shots from the same spot
quiz.explain: Using only one shot type from one place makes every photo look the same.

levels.title: Share your work and keep going

lessons.title: Share your work before it feels ready
lessons.content:
Sharing early means showing your work to a few people while it's still unfinished, instead of hiding it until it's "perfect." Think of cooking for guests. A good cook tastes the curry while it's still on the stove and adds salt then. If you only taste it after serving, it's too late to fix. Sharing early is tasting while you can still change things.

Why does it matter? Because when you work alone for weeks, you stop seeing your own mistakes. You know what you meant, so you can't tell if others will understand. Many people never share at all, waiting for a perfect day that never comes, and their work stays in a drawer. Sharing early gets you useful feedback while changes are easy, and it builds the habit of finishing and showing, which is how you actually grow.

Here's how to do it safely. Step one: share small and early. A rough sketch, the first paragraph, three photos. Not the whole thing after a month. Step two: choose the right first audience. Start with two or three people you trust, like a friend, a sibling or a teacher, not a big public group. Step three: ask a specific question instead of "Is it good?" Try: "Where did you get bored?", "What's the first thing you notice?" or "Which of these two photos do you prefer and why?" Specific questions get useful answers.

Step four: share on a schedule, not when you feel ready. For example, "Every Friday I'll show one thing I made this week." You'll never feel fully ready, so let the calendar decide. Step five: as you get more comfortable, share with bigger groups, like a class display or a small Facebook post.

Meet Sabbir from Noakhali. He spent two months drawing a 20-page comic, showing it to nobody. When he finally gave it to his friends, they all said the same thing: "We didn't understand who the main character was until page 8." Fixing it meant redrawing almost half the comic. For his next comic, he showed his friend Rafi just the first 3 pages and asked, "Is it clear who the hero is?" Rafi said the hero and the villain looked too similar. Sabbir changed one character's hair in ten minutes. The new comic was clearer and finished in half the time.

The common mistake is sharing too early with too many people, like posting a messy first draft publicly and getting hurt by random comments. Early sharing works best with a small, trusted group and a clear question.

Remember: show small pieces early to a few trusted people, and ask them one specific question.
key_points: Sharing early means showing unfinished work while changes are still easy.
Start with two or three trusted people, not a big public group.
Ask a specific question like "Where did you get bored?" instead of "Is it good?"
Share on a schedule, like every Friday, instead of waiting to feel ready.
lessons.tip: Write your question before you share, on a slip of paper or at the top of your message. It keeps feedback focused on what you need.
lessons.task: Pick something unfinished you've made, like a drawing, a few lines of writing or 3 photos. Send it to one trusted person today with one specific question.

quiz.q: Why is sharing early useful?
options: It makes your work finish itself
It means you never need to edit
You get feedback while changes are still easy
quiz.explain: Like tasting curry on the stove, early feedback lets you fix things before it's too late.

quiz.q: Which is the most useful question to ask when sharing?
quiz.explain: A specific question gets a specific, useful answer.

quiz.q: What did Sabbir do differently with his second comic?
options: He hid it for three months
He posted it publicly on day one
He asked his teacher to draw it
He showed 3 pages to a friend early with a specific question
quiz.explain: Showing a small piece early let him fix a problem in ten minutes instead of redrawing half the comic.

lessons.title: Handle creative critique
lessons.content:
Critique is when someone tells you what works and what doesn't in your work. It's like a cricket coach watching you bat. He doesn't say "you're a bad player." He says "your front foot isn't moving forward." That's information you can use. Good critique is about the work, not about you.

Why does it matter? Because nobody improves fast alone. Other people spot things you can't see, like a confusing sentence or a crooked horizon. But critique can hurt, and if it hurts too much, people either stop sharing or argue with everyone and learn nothing. Learning to take critique calmly is what separates people who keep improving from people who get stuck.

Here's how to handle it. Step one: listen fully and don't defend. Your only job while they speak is to understand. Don't explain "but I meant..." Just say "okay" and take notes. Step two: say thank you, even if it stings. They spent time on your work. Step three: ask a follow-up question to get specifics. If someone says "the ending is weak," ask "what would make it stronger?" or "where did you stop caring?"

Step four: wait before deciding. Feelings are loudest in the first hour. Look at the notes again the next day. Step five: sort the comments into three piles. Fix now: if two or more people say the same thing, it's almost always a real problem. Try it: a single interesting suggestion you can test. Ignore: comments that are about taste, or that would turn your work into something you don't want. You don't have to obey every comment. You only have to consider it.

Meet Tania from Pabna. She sang a Rabindra Sangeet at a school event and asked her music teacher for feedback. The teacher said, "Your voice is sweet, but you rushed the second verse and your breathing broke the long notes." Tania's face went hot, and she almost said, "I was nervous!" Instead she said, "Thank you, where exactly should I breathe?" The teacher marked two breathing spots on her lyrics sheet. The next morning Tania practised just those two lines ten times. At the next event, her friend recorded it, and Tania could hear the difference herself.

The common mistake is taking critique of the work as an attack on yourself. "The colours are muddy" doesn't mean "you're a bad artist." It means "the colours are muddy," and that's fixable. Separate the work from yourself, and critique becomes free lessons.

Remember: listen without defending, ask for specifics, wait a day, then fix what several people agree on.
key_points: Good critique is about the work, not about you.
Listen fully, don't defend, and say thank you.
Ask follow-up questions to get specific advice.
Wait a day, then fix what several people agree on and test the rest.
lessons.tip: When getting feedback, hold a pen and write while they talk. Writing keeps your mouth busy so you don't start defending.
lessons.task: Ask one person to give you one thing that works and one thing to improve in something you made recently. Write their exact words down and reply only with "thank you" and one follow-up question.

quiz.q: What should you do while someone gives you critique?
options: Explain what you meant right away
Listen fully without defending and take notes
Point out mistakes in their work
quiz.explain: Your job while they speak is to understand, not to argue.

quiz.q: When should you almost always fix something?
options: When two or more people say the same thing
Only when your best friend says it
Only if it's about the title
quiz.explain: When several people notice the same problem, it is very likely real.

quiz.q: How did Tania respond to her music teacher's critique?
options: She stopped singing for a month
She said thank you and asked exactly where to breathe
quiz.explain: A thank you plus a specific question turned the critique into clear practice steps.

lessons.title: Originality, influence and credit
lessons.content:
Every creator learns from others. That's influence, and it's normal. Copying is taking someone's work and showing it as your own. Originality isn't making something from nothing. It's mixing many influences with your own life until the result is clearly yours. Think of how you learned handwriting: first by tracing letters, then copying your teacher's, until now your writing looks like nobody else's.

Why does it matter? Because if you think you must be 100% original, you'll freeze, since nothing comes from nothing. But if you copy someone and claim it as yours, you can get into real trouble: losing marks, being called a cheat, having posts reported, and losing people's trust. Knowing the difference lets you learn freely from others while staying honest and building your own style.

Here's how to do it right. Rule one: copy to learn, privately. Copying a famous painting or a favourite song is a great way to practise. Keep it in your practice notebook, or if you share it, say clearly "My practice copy of a painting by Zainul Abedin." Rule two: when you share, give credit. If you used someone's photo, idea, music or quote, name them: "Photo: Rafi Ahmed" or "Inspired by a reel from @artbyNila." Never post someone else's photo or drawing as if you made it.

Rule three: steal from many, not from one. If you learn from only one artist, you become a copy of them. If you learn a colour idea from one, a drawing style from another, and a story idea from your grandmother, the mix becomes yours. Rule four: add your own life. Your town, your family, your language, your jokes. Nobody else has those. That's where your originality really comes from.

Meet Nusrat from Dinajpur. She loved a famous illustrator's style and started drawing exactly like her. She posted one drawing without mentioning the artist, and people commented, "This looks just like that illustrator's work." She felt embarrassed. She changed her approach. She kept practising that illustrator's line work, but she also studied the colours of rickshaw art and drew scenes from her own village: litchi trees, her cousin's goat, the evening bazar. She also wrote "Inspired by" in her captions whenever she borrowed something specific. Within a few months, people started saying "That's a Nusrat drawing" without seeing her name.

The common mistake is thinking that changing a few small things makes copying okay. Flipping a photo, changing a colour or swapping two words is still copying. If the main idea and look are someone else's, give credit or don't share it as yours.

Remember: learn from many people, give credit whenever you borrow, and mix in your own life to make it yours.
key_points: Influence is normal; copying means showing someone else's work as yours.
Copy to practise privately, and give clear credit when you share.
Learn from many people so the mix becomes your own style.
Changing small details doesn't make a copy original.
lessons.tip: When you save someone's work for inspiration, save their name with it right away, like in the file name. Then giving credit later takes two seconds.
lessons.task: Pick a drawing, photo or poem you admire. Write down three things you like about it. Then make one small piece using one of those things plus something from your own life.

quiz.q: What is the difference between influence and copying?
options: Influence is illegal, copying is fine
Influence is learning from others; copying is showing someone else's work as your own
quiz.explain: Learning from others is normal. Claiming their work as yours is the problem.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to build your own style?
options: Learn from many people and add your own life
Never look at anyone else's work
Flip other people's photos so they look different
quiz.explain: Mixing many influences with your own experiences makes the result truly yours.

quiz.q: What helped Nusrat develop her own recognizable style?
options: Copying the illustrator even more closely
Mixing rickshaw art colours and scenes from her own village, and giving credit
Removing the illustrator's name from her posts
quiz.explain: She learned from several sources, added her own life, and credited what she borrowed.

lessons.title: Build a creative habit that lasts
lessons.content:
A creative practice is a small, regular habit of making things, like brushing your teeth, but for your imagination. It's not about waiting for big bursts of inspiration. It's about showing up a little, often. Think of a mango tree. You don't water it once with a whole tank and leave it for a month. You water it a little every day, and over years it grows big and gives fruit.

Why does it matter? Because most people make things in bursts: a great week of drawing, then nothing for two months. Each time they restart, they've lost their skill and confidence, and it feels hard again. A steady practice keeps your skills warm, gives you a pile of work to learn from, and makes creating feel normal instead of scary. Ten minutes every day beats three hours once a month.

Here's how to build one. Step one: start tiny. Pick something so small you can't say no, like one sketch, five lines of writing, or one photo a day. You can always do more, but the minimum is what counts. Step two: attach it to something you already do daily. "After I drink tea in the evening, I draw for ten minutes." The tea becomes your reminder. Step three: track it. Draw a simple calendar and put a tick for every day you make something. Seeing a row of ticks makes you want to keep it going.

Step four: plan for bad days. On exam days or when you're sick, do a "minimum version," like a 1-minute doodle. It keeps the habit alive. If you miss a day, don't miss two. Step five: finish small projects. Every month, choose one small project to complete, like a 6-photo story or a short comic. Finishing things is what builds confidence.

Meet Rafi from Tangail. He loved drawing but only drew when he felt inspired, maybe twice a month. He kept feeling "rusty." In January he made a rule: one small sketch every night after Isha prayer, at least 5 minutes. He kept a tick chart on his wall. Some nights he drew just a cup or his shoe. In March, during exams, he did 1-minute doodles. By June, he had over 150 sketches. Looking at the first page and the last page side by side, he couldn't believe how much better he'd become. His art teacher asked him to design the cover of the school magazine.

The common mistake is starting too big, like "I'll draw for two hours every day." It works for three days, then life gets busy and you quit completely. Small and daily always beats big and rare.

Remember: start tiny, attach it to a daily habit, track it, and never miss two days in a row.
key_points: A creative practice is a small, regular habit, not waiting for inspiration.
Start so small you can't say no, like one sketch a day.
Attach it to something you already do daily, and track it with ticks.
On bad days do a minimum version; never miss two days in a row.
lessons.tip: Keep your sketchbook or notebook out on the table, open, with a pen on it. If it's hidden in a drawer, you'll skip it.
lessons.task: Choose your tiny daily practice and the habit you'll attach it to, like "after evening tea, one sketch." Draw a 30-day tick chart and do day one right now.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, which is better?
quiz.explain: Small, regular practice keeps your skills warm and builds up a lot of work over time.

quiz.q: What should you do on a busy exam day?
options: Do a minimum version, like a 1-minute doodle
Do double the next day instead
quiz.explain: A tiny minimum version keeps the habit alive even on bad days.

quiz.q: How did Rafi build his drawing habit?
options: He drew for two hours every day
He did a 5-minute sketch every night after Isha, tracked with ticks
quiz.explain: A tiny goal attached to a daily routine, plus a tick chart, gave him 150 sketches by June.
